change.summary: Google designated the Places, Directions and Distance Matrix web services as 'Legacy'. From 2025-03-01 a Cloud project that had not ALREADY enabled them can never enable them. Projects already using them keep full support and saw no behavioural change at all.

spec.note: The new Places API has a Discovery document and protos; the legacy web service never had either. Same pattern as Twitter and OpenWeather — the surface being retired is the one with no machine-readable contract.

changelog.note: It shipped as a PRICING announcement. The earliest artifact is a billing FAQ; the Places release notes say nothing about it, and it does not appear on Google's own deprecations page even now. A crawler watching the obvious API channels would have missed it entirely — which is a real finding about where announcements actually live.

contract.note: Not detectable by calling. Probed 2026-09-19: all seven legacy endpoints still serve normal JSON. The break is invisible from the wire because it is a control-plane restriction on project provisioning, not a change to the API's behaviour.

notes: DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED FROM SCORING, and the exclusion is the point. Nothing was turned off. Google invented a lifecycle stage called 'Legacy' that is explicitly NOT 'Deprecated', which avoids starting the 12-month decommission clock in its terms of service; its own wording is 'there is no date yet for when this will happen'. Calling this a breaking change would inflate the dataset. It is kept as a record of a judgement call and because the narrow break it DID cause is instructive: every new developer, fresh CI or staging project, and open-source library whose users create new projects broke on 2025-03-01, which is exactly when the linked issues cluster, while existing projects noticed nothing. Also note the legacy docs were not re-badged with the Legacy banner until some point after the effective date — the 2025-02-03 capture carries no warning whatsoever.
